About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?
B rett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.
“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”
Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.
High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”
The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”
It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”

Artist Sally J. Han is an exacting painter with a meticulous eye. Her detailed, colorful works depict some of life’s most ordinary moments—scrolling on a phone, peeling fruit—yet are juxtaposed with surrealist elements. Han often does this through scale. In Satellite of Love , for instance, a diminutive figure wearing a hanbok sits on a rock gazing up at an impossibly large moon that takes over the composition. It’s something we’d imagine many of us doing; however, in Han’s hands, it takes on a fantastical feel that invites many interpretations.
Han has a multicultural background, and art has served as a bridge between cultures. “From an early age, I thought of drawing as a form of communication,” she tells My Modern Met. “Having grown up in South Korea and China, and later moving to the U.S., I sometimes relied on simple sketches to express myself when I wasn’t yet familiar with the language of each country. I had always enjoyed drawing as a child, but living in different countries made it feel less like a talent and more like my own familiar way of expressing myself.”
We follow the same figure throughout Han’s work. Like the artist, the figure exists in different landscapes, including a desert sunset, a verdant tropical garden, and on a large porch with a yard. Carefully rendered elements dot the composition, like animals, tipped-over soda cans, and a pair of eyeglasses held loosely in a hand. Individually, the common objects aren’t anything special. But in Han’s visual language, they become layered and lyrical, touching on ideas of tradition and our own mythology, and ultimately shaped by our own analysis.
“I find that the familiarity and comfort of everyday life can often feel surprisingly new when viewed from a different perspective,” she explains. “I think what I enjoy most is discovering those moments.” Cultures different from her own have always fascinated her. “But what I find even more interesting is the sense of connection we can share despite our differences. I’ve always been drawn to the human side of things, and I think that naturally finds its way into my paintings.”
Han recently concluded a solo exhibition titled Gazing at Lee Art Consulting in Seoul. She’s currently working on paintings that will debut in spring 2027 at Dan Yoshii in New York City.

Painter Reggie Burrows Hodges brings a contemporary perspective to 17th-century European art in Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Passions , opening at the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles. The exhibition features paintings inspired by works in the Getty’s collection , exploring the violence and theatricality behind historical narratives. It is part of a three-venue presentation that also includes exhibitions at the California African American Museum and Art + Practice .
Born in Compton in 1965, Hodges draws on Old Master paintings to examine power, memory, and human experience. He often begins with the compositions of historical works, then reshapes their themes through his own visual language. His paintings emerge from black grounds, with figures defined by soft, gestural marks and richly rendered surroundings. The dark palettes and hazy contours evoke the uncertainty of memory, giving ordinary gestures a heightened emotional presence.
At the Getty, Hodges responds to three Italian paintings: Orazio Gentileschi’s Lot and His Daughters and Danaë and the Shower of Gold , and Artemisia Gentileschi’s Lucretia . Each work contains dramatic narratives shaped by violence, vulnerability, and power. Hodges draws out these underlying tensions through atmospheric compositions that favor psychological presence over naturalistic detail. His interpretations offer a contemporary reading of the original paintings without losing sight of their emotional complexity.
The presentation extends to the California African American Museum, where Reggie Burrows Hodges: A Theater of Miracles explores further connections to historical painting. Several works take inspiration from the Getty’s collection, including Jacopo Bassano’s 16th-century painting T he Miracle of the Quail . Hodges reworks the drama of these earlier compositions while directing attention toward the everyday gestures that give his scenes their emotional weight.

items.desc: The rocket stage was caught mid air using huge mechanical arms nicknamed "chopsticks".
items.text:
'Can you believe it?': SpaceX catches part of its Starship rocket on return to Earth
SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its huge Starship rocket for the first time, after a flight lasting 22-and-a-half hours.
The rocket returned to Earth and hovered near its launch tower, whose mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - then secured it.
The company had hoped to catch the bottom part of the rocket as well, but this was aborted a few minutes after the launch on Friday.
SpaceX needs to reliably recover both parts of Starship so that it can fly repeatedly and drastically reduce costs.
The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday
There were loud cheers from SpaceX staff who were watching the flight as the rocket returned to the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas.
This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable.
The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:47 local time (19:47 GMT) on Friday.
The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half-minutes later when it returned.
But the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.
Elon Musk later posted on X that the booster had been "slightly low on fuel".
The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames
The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.
The Ship completed 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower.
SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But this was the first time the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has been grabbed by the "chopsticks".
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.
Any problems would have resulted in the ship being brought down in the ocean in the same way as the booster.

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.

items.text:
Tirana, Albania, has become one of Europe’s fastest-growing cities. This growth has sparked a real estate boom, but locals worry about losing green areas and public spaces. Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) has addressed these issues with its proposal for an upcoming development on Rinia Park, in the heart of Tirana.
Named Fountain Plaza Tirana, the project won over designs presented by four other international firms. Conceived as a mixed-use building, Fountain Plaza Tirana will stand several feet above Rinia Park, preserving and expanding the public park area while making room for a new hotel, apartments, offices, and cultural spaces.
The building evokes a dense cloud formation above the park. To achieve this, layers of rounded, perforated white terraces rest on slim columns, while two wider structures at opposite ends of the building house the elevators that provide floor access. To avoid breaking with the “floating” concept, these elements are clad in flute glass to let light shine through and onto the park.
“We have reimagined urban living in three dimensions—not as a vertical extrusion or a tower competing for attention on the skyline, but as a cloud of homes hovering above the park,” said BIG founder Bjarke Ingels told Dezeen . “Rather than diminishing the park or displacing public life, the building enhances and accommodates both.”
As such, Fountain Plaza Tirana will also feature an open-access library, a covered public auditorium, and community facilities. In addition to the design that lets pedestrians move freely across the park, this aims to make the building’s ground floor a bustling gathering place for city dwellers and visitors alike.
The design also accounts for Tirana’s weather, particularly its hot summers. The structures bring shade to a public park without completely blocking sunlight. Meanwhile, the water features, described as an “inverted fountain,” can cool the area with the effect of a light drizzle. The water used comes from a closed-loop system. With this, the water collected from the building and the green areas at the bottom is stored, filtered, and returned to the park below.
While a building timeline has yet to be announced, it will surely be interesting to see how Fountain Plaza Tirana takes shape. items.text:
From the first day of his life, little infant Adnan has suffered a seizure roughly every 13 minutes.
One can only imagine the reactions from his Dubai hospital bedside when, having received a still-experimental drug, his seizures stopped for the day.
And for the week, and the week after that—and the week after that.
The story comes via the Khaleej Times , which reported that the Dubai Health Authority (DHA) granted an application from King’s College Hospital London in Dubai through a “compassionate use” pathway for the use of a drug that is otherwise not approved for commercial use.
Called ABS-1230, the experimental oral medication targets abnormal activity in an ion channel associated with the “extremely rare” form of genetic epilepsy Adnan suffers from.
According to data from the treatment’s developer, Adnan is the youngest patient in the world to receive ABS-1230 and only the second infant to be given the experimental medication.
At the Dubai hospital, sequencing of Adnan’s entire genome revealed a gene variant associated with the seizures and allowed the medical team to identify ABS-1230 as a potential treatment option.
Led by Professor Ubaid Shah, consultant pediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the hospital, the drug was administered on September 14th. The success was so profound and immediate that Adnan was discharged from the hospital with his family just a week later, without a single seizure having been recorded during that time.
“This is an exceptional moment for us, and it highlights what precision medicine can achieve when we are able to identify the genetic cause of a disease and choose a treatment that targets the mechanism linked to it,” Professor Shah told the Times.
Adnan suffered no clinical seizures at his October 11th follow-up. The hospital said he continues to be seizure-free as of November 2nd, and the infant is finally beginning to pass some early development milestones.
“Despite the encouraging response, we will continue to monitor his condition closely to assess whether the results are sustained and whether the experimental treatment is safe,” Professor Shah said.
Indeed, Shah and his colleagues stressed that the treatment is still experimental and requires more research before it can be approved for use by the public. That being said, however, Adnan’s response to it couldn’t have been more positive.

items.title: German Renaissance Master Albrecht Altdorfer Pioneered Landscape Painting. A Work Previously Unknown to Scholars Just Emerged After 70 Years in a Private Collection
items.desc: Painted around 1520, the newly identified painting is one of only three pure landscapes painted in oil by the artist. It depicts a lush forest scene with castle ruins and a rainbow emerging from stormy skies
items.text:
For nearly seven decades, a small 16th-century painting of a forest hung in a private collection in Switzerland, unbeknownst to art historians. Now, the 500-year-old work has emerged into the limelight, newly attributed to Albrecht Altdorfer , a German Renaissance artist who pioneered landscape painting.
Measuring roughly nine inches long by eight inches wide and dating from around 1520, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky will head to auction at Sotheby’s in London on December 9.
“Every inch of this intimate picture is imbued with an intense mood that transcends its scale … It somehow still feels as modern and immediate as it would have appeared to those seeing it when it was first painted,” George Gordon , co-chair of Sotheby’s Old Masters department, says in a statement . “To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field.”
The painting, which does not appear in Altdorfer’s catalogue raisonné and was only identified earlier this year, is expected to sell for up to $6.6 million. “We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon tells the Art Newspaper ’s Catherine Hickley. “It could fetch more than our estimate.”
Until its discovery, scholars knew of just two oil landscapes by Altdorfer, both held in major European museums: Landscape With a Footbridge at London’s National Gallery and Landscape of the Danube Near Regensburg at Munich’s Alte Pinakothek . No Altdorfer painting has appeared on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery acquired Christ Taking Leave of His Mother .
Painted in oil on vellum, A Thickly Wooded Landscape is the smallest and most densely forested of Altdorfer’s surviving landscapes in any medium, including engravings, etchings and drawings. In the foreground, tangled evergreens and mossy undergrowth rise without a single human figure in sight, while a distant castle perches atop a rocky outcrop on the right. Overhead, heavy clouds part just enough to reveal a faint glow from the sun, whose light catches a delicate rainbow arching behind the trees.

items.title: Florida Is Facing Its Worst Dengue Outbreak in Decades, With at Least 524 Locally Acquired Cases. Here's What to Know
items.desc: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
items.text:
McKenzie Prillaman | Assistant Digital Editor, Science & Innovation
This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025.
Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis.
Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.
“It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”
Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions , where these biting insects thrive, than in temperate climates.
Around three in four infected people are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, nausea and rash. Muscle and joint pain is another common symptom, which is why the disease is sometimes called “breakbone fever.” Symptoms usually appear within two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito and clear up after a week or two.
However, one in four dengue cases becomes severe. Those symptoms include extreme abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and blood in vomit or stool, and anyone experiencing them should seek medical care. These signs often appear after the fever goes away, and people who have previously been infected are at a greater risk of severe dengue.
Individuals who recover from dengue can continue feeling fatigued for several weeks.
Although dengue vaccines exist , none are currently approved for use in the United States. They’re authorized in nations where the disease is more common, such as Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand.

Property sales that complete on this day have a lower median price. Air fares are cheaper. Weddings are non-existent. And motor collisions increase. How did it become so mired in superstition?
“I have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.”
Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck.
Today is the third Friday 13th in 2026 – the maximum number of times this date can occur in any year in the Gregorian calendar, and the only such year this decade. The last year with three Friday 13ths was 2015. But where does western wariness of this date come from – and is there any evidence that it does bring bad luck?
The origins of the superstition are not entirely clear. Some believe the number 13 to be unlucky in itself, thanks to a mix of religious, folkloric and cultural traditions. In Norse mythology, for example, triskaidekaphobia – fear or avoidance of the number 13 – can be traced back to the story of Loki , a “trickster” or god of mischief, who crashed a banquet in Valhalla, becoming the 13th guest and then murdering the host’s popular servant, Fimafeng.
In Christianity, there is also the idea that Judas, the disciple who betrayed Jesus, was the 13th to sit at the table for the Last Supper , with Jesus’s crucifixion the following day (and which is itself believed to have taken place on a Friday).
Others attribute Friday 13th’s supposed bad luck to the Knights Templar, hundreds of whom were arrested for heresy on Friday 13 October 1307 . A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope , including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.
"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell , ESA's director of science, said in a statement . "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."
Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.
Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.
A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.
Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These " Einstein rings " ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein , who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.
In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

items.desc: The small decrease seems to stem partially from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a major global chokepoint for oil transportation. Scientists say that the decline will not last without the accelerated deployment of renewable energies
items.text:
In 2020, humans hunkered down amid the Covid-19 pandemic, contributing to an unprecedented 7 percent decrease in global fossil fuel emissions , according to the Global Carbon Project, an international collaboration that releases annual reports on emissions trends. For the first time since then, emissions are expected to fall again, although to a lesser degree.
Global Carbon Project researchers predict that in 2026, countries will have emitted 42.1 billion U.S. tons of planet-warming carbon dioxide, a 0.4 percent decrease compared with the previous year. That’s partly because of growing solar and wind power, but also a surge in oil prices and supply chain issues sparked by the United States-Israel war with Iran.
The team described these findings in a preprint report, which has not been peer-reviewed, released on November 10 in the journal Earth System Data Science . Some of the scientists also published an analysis in the journal Nature Climate Change .
“A decline in fossil [carbon dioxide] emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” says report and study co-author Pierre Friedlingstein , a climate scientist at the University of Exeter in England, in a statement . “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”
According to Friedlingstein and colleagues’ calculations, emissions from oil and gas are projected to decline this year by 1.9 and 0.3 percent, respectively. However, that’s partially offset by a 0.6 percent rise in emissions from coal. (Burning coal generates more pollution than oil or gas.)
In 2020, levels of methane—the second-largest contributor to climate change—surprisingly spiked. Earlier this year, researchers reported that the unexpected surge was caused by dynamics in the atmosphere and natural sources of the gas, including wetlands.
China emits around one-third of the world’s fossil emissions, making it the country that produces the most carbon dioxide. This year, its emissions declined overall, despite a small bump in coal pollution. items.text:
Some of the “very last wild and healthy ecosystems” unblemished by humans have been discovered in the remote atolls of the Pacific Ocean teeming with life.
Scientists wrote in a new study that, although humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, a few very remote islands of coral may be the exceptions.
Researchers described the two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located in the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.
The two atolls—roughly midway between Hawaii and the Philippines—are now part of a newly created National Marine Sanctuary.
“Bikar and Bokak are not just treasures for the Marshall Islands but for the entire planet, a gift from the community of Utirik Atoll, which has traditionally and vigilantly safeguarded these fragile ecosystems for decades,” said study first author Dr. Alan Friedlander.
Bikar and Bokak are the northernmost atolls in the Marshall Islands, lying around 72 and 239 miles from the nearest inhabited atoll, respectively.
The research team in 2023 began conducting extensive monitoring of local land, sea, and sky ecosystems, assessing sea- and shorebird populations, and vegetation.
They conducted surveys of turtle nesting, coral reefs and fish assemblages using scuba, underwater video, deep-sea camera deployments, and a submarine.
Dr. Friedlander, a marine ecologist at the University of Hawai’i, says the extensive surveying of the ecosystems offers an unparalleled glimpse into how they function with only minimal human influence.
Two years after the assessment, some 18,500 square miles around the atolls were declared the country’s first national marine sanctuary.
“These atolls have extensive seabird colonies, mature native vegetation, active turtle nesting, high fish numbers with large predators… and surprisingly diverse and poorly-known deep-sea communities.”
For instance, they counted over a dozen breeding seabird colonies, 266 groups of reef fish, 79 groups of deep-sea fishes, and 15 groups of open-water predators—including sharks, jacks, and wahoo.
Fully 14 of the observed groups haven’t previously been recorded in the Marshall Islands, and two might be species new to science.

items.text:
Portrait of Abraham Lincoln. (Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons , Public domain)
For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. Cataloged as a crowd scene, the photograph showed spectators gathered around a platform in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing among the crowd. The photograph captured the president at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, the same day he delivered the Gettysburg Address.
Cobb joined the U.S. National Archives in 1936. Her work focused on historical photographs, including Civil War images. When she examined the glass plate, she suspected it might depict the Gettysburg ceremony. A tall flag helped her locate the speakers’ platform. She then enlarged that section to examine the figures more closely.
The result revealed a small, bare-headed man with a beard and a distinctive profile. Cobb identified him as Lincoln. She also recognized Ward Hill Lamon, the president’s bodyguard and the ceremony’s chief marshal, along with Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin. Other figures have been proposed as members of Lincoln’s party, though some identifications remain disputed.
The photograph belonged to a collection associated with Civil War photographer Mathew Brady . The U.S. government purchased Brady’s photographic collection in the 1870s, and the material eventually entered the National Archives. However, the photographer who took this particular image remains unknown. The glass plate had also lost roughly a quarter of its upper-left corner, further complicating its examination.
Cobb estimated that the photograph was taken around noon, when Lincoln arrived at the platform. His famous address came approximately three hours later. The image does not capture the speech itself. Instead, it offers a rare glimpse of Lincoln at the ceremony before he delivered one of the most enduring speeches in American history.
The discovery became public on February 12, 1953, Lincoln’s birthday. The Gettysburg Times reported the finding, and Life magazine later published the image. Early coverage approached the identification cautiously because the figure’s face was blurred. Lincoln occupies only a small portion of the original photograph, making historical context essential to the identification.
Cobb’s discovery reflected years of experience examining archival images.

items.text:
The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China.
Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. It can then be rapidly released to power a turbine and discharge that green energy back into the grid.
China has received numerous plaudits for its rapid adoption of renewable energy at both scale and speed, and this new facility in Qinghai Province brings in a key missing element to the renewable build-out: grid-scale battery storage for when the Sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing.
Not that either of those happen very often in Qinghai, which encompasses parts of the Tibetan Plateau, and Mongolia-like grasslands and desert, where both sun and wind are famously relentless.
Described as “the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity,” the facility is rated at 600 megawatt-hours, and will substantially back up the renewable contribution to the regional power grid by providing 10 hours of continual power supply when necessary. Additionally, it was built with its own solar farm, rated at 250MW.
LAES works by turning ordinary air into a liquid, keeping that liquid in insulated tanks, and then converting it back into electricity when needed.
When electricity is plentiful, it powers machinery that draws in air, compresses it and cools it to extremely low temperatures of around -190°C. At this point, the air becomes a liquid, taking up far less space than it did as a gas.
When power is needed, the liquid air is pumped to high pressure and warmed. As it warms, it rapidly expands back into a gas and can be used to spin a turbine connected to an electricity generator, sending power back to the grid.
A cool party trick is how the system utilizes the excess heat and cold: it stores both for heating and cooling the air as needed, reducing energy consumption and environmental disturbance.

Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

items.desc: According to Peruvian officials, the three European travelers—including one who's been identified as a "renowned tarantula researcher"—could have made around $1.68 million from the creepy-crawly loot
items.text:
Authorities in Peru say they have foiled a plot to smuggle more than 3,000 tarantulas—including species not yet described in scientific publications—out of the country.
After receiving an anonymous tip , officials intercepted three travelers—two German citizens and one Polish citizen—at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima as they were checking in at the boarding area. When they searched the travelers’ luggage, they found thousands of eggs, hatchlings and adult spiders hidden in socks, according to a November 4 statement from the National Forest and Wildlife Service of Peru (SERFOR).
“We noticed that some of them were moving,” Cora Suárez , a SERFOR forest and wildlife control technician who works at the airport, tells the Agence France-Presse . “There were small ones and large ones.”
Workers used slender wooden sticks to gently brush the spiders into clear plastic containers. Once officials are done investigating them, the tarantulas will be taken to an authorized breeding center.
The travelers were trying to fly to Germany. Instead, they were detained by the Peruvian National Police’s environmental crimes unit and now face criminal charges.
Officials have not released the names of the individuals. However, one of the travelers was a “renowned tarantula researcher,” according to the statement, per a translation by the New York Times ’ Amanda Holpuch.
Authorities suspect the individuals were smuggling the spiders for private collections, research and the exotic pet trade. Suárez tells the AFP that one tarantula can sell for roughly $560 in Europe, meaning the smugglers could have made around $1.68 million from the more than 3,000 tarantulas they had hidden in their suitcases.
The spiders originated from several different parts of Peru, including the cities of Cajamarca, Cusco and Junín, and the regions of La Libertad and Loreto. Officials are still trying to pinpoint all the species in the loot but said it included several brightly colored creatures.
Wildlife trafficking is the world’s fourth-largest form of organized crime, with an estimated annual value of up to $20 billion .
So far, officials have identified Thrixopelma lagunas , also known as the Peruvian blue zebra or the blue birdeater. Authorities also found members of the Pamphobeteus genus, which are among the largest tarantulas in the world.

On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days.
Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission.
The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks.
“For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. They maintained their habitat. They grew crops, and they carried out simulated Mars operations.”
After the speech, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway , who had just completed a mission at the International Space Station, knocked on the door to the Mars habitat, called out “trick or treat” and opened it to reveal the crew’s smiling faces. Since then, the analog astronauts have been participating in post-mission evaluations and debriefs that, along with the data collected during their year in the simulated environment, will help inform future missions to Mars and those closer to home, per a NASA statement .
“Most days, we had things that were scheduled, from maintenance and science and engineering activities and some operational activities. So, we often do extravehicular activities, also known as EVAs or spacewalks,” Elder, who was the mission’s commander and test pilot, tells CNN News Central . “We would do drone and rover operations where we control certain equipment outside of the habitat, and we would practice additional data collection for both human health and behavioral sciences.”

“Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.”
One can only imagine the pause, double-take, or request for clarity which followed this comment, made by a woman’s elderly aunt in the midst of an effort to clean out her East Village apartment.
Yet as the woman, who revealed herself only as Betsy, rummaged around in that closet 4 years later, she found an oil painting of undulating hills, with soft earthen colors reminiscent of the female form, which is now known to be Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, painted by the Mother of Modernism in 1930.
Its rediscovery has been hailed as “a once-in-a-lifetime moment, and absolutely thrilling.”
Soon to be auctioned at Christie’s where it’s expected to garner around $3 million, the story of its provenance first broke at the New York Post , who talked to Betsy about the fateful closet-cleaning
Her aunt, she said, was an “extremely intelligent” former foreign service member who had received the painting from Georgia O’Keeffe’s Manhattan art dealer in 1963 as a graduation present from her parents. At the time time it cost $3,800.
Her aunt loved the painting, and hung it in the apartment for years. It ended up in the closet after she noticed that an evening during a bridge game, one of the players kept his eyes fixed on it for far too long.
“I think she was fully aware of its value … she recognized that it was an expression of her financial position,” Betsy told the Post.
She decided to take it down so as to not draw attention to herself during similar soirées. Amid her fur coats the painting sat, even after her niece came over in 2022 to help clean out the apartment as the woman prepared to enter hospice care. It was only after her aunt passed away that Betsy followed up on the comment of the “O’Keeffe in the closet” that she found it, still in its original box marked “The Downtown Gallery, 51st St.”

items.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms
items.desc: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
items.text:
In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake .
The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm.
“It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.”
Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science .
To better understand what happened, the team homed in on two major events: the Johnson River slide in August 2017 that moved about 4.5 million cubic meters of dirt and rock, and the Redstone River slide in August 2018 that sent roughly 18 million cubic meters of debris tumbling down. Satellite imagery captured between 1980 and 2020 and field studies revealed some odd characteristics, the team found.

Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires and overheating," said Fisher.

Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".

items.text:

In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external

A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease.
Doctors at Franciscan Health used bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor to treat a 40-year-old woman with aplastic anemia
The patient, with a decade-long history of the disease, received the bone marrow stem cell transplant on April 18, after her disease progressed from stable to severe, despite multiple lines of therapy.
Because her disease no longer responded to medication, her care team pursued a transplant to replace her failing marrow with healthy blood-forming stem cells.
Six months after the transplant, the donor marrow has taken hold and restored her blood counts.
She no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions and has achieved full donor chimerism, meaning her blood and immune system are now produced entirely by the donor’s stem cells, without complications.
For non-malignant conditions including severe aplastic anemia, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, and other inherited or acquired bone marrow failure disorders, bone marrow-derived stem cells are widely regarded as the preferred stem cell source over peripheral blood stem cells (PBSCs), and the source of choice for non-malignant diseases.
“Bone marrow transplantation for severe aplastic anemia has been performed since the 1970s using living related and unrelated donors.
“To our knowledge, this is the first reported transplant of deceased organ donor bone marrow for severe aplastic anemia,” said Felix Mensah, MD, the treating physician at Franciscan Health.
“This case shows why continued innovation in transplant medicine matters, and why we need more donor options, so that every patient with a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder has access to potentially curative therapy.”
“Reaching the first non-malignant transplant is a defining moment,” said Kevin Caldwell , Co-Founder and CEO of Ossium, which maintains a marrow bank.
“By recovering and banking bone marrow from organ donors, we can consistently optimize treatment outcomes.”

After 100 years, Gretchen Sollo had a major first: a surprise birthday party, thrown by the Lowe’s employees she sees every day.
Following a stroke, Sollo turned to the aisles of Lowe’s for her daily walk and to keep out of the weather in Bradley, Illinois. She’s since walked an estimated 1,500 miles over five years, creating a daily ritual and friendships with staff members that stretched around the store.
Store associates check on her number of laps and even challenge her to races, joining her on her walks around the store. If there’s ever a day Sollo doesn’t show up, staff members notice and worry.
Store manager Joe Jackson gave her the honorary title of “store mom.”
Once Jackson and staff found out Sollo was turning 100 on November 1, 2026, they knew they had to do something special.
When Sollo showed up for her daily laps on October 30, she was joined by Jackson. Jackson guided Sollo over to a decorated aisle where a blue carpet led to an arch of birthday balloons, a cake and a personalized Lowe’s vest for Sollo. The aisle was lined by around 50 associates (some who came on their day off), friends, family and Sollo’s son Hugh.
“I never wanted a birthday party,” Sollo told People in an exclusive interview, adding “Means I missed out on a lot, I guess.”
A woman who spent a century working, raising a family, and staying active finally took a moment to allow others to show how much they cared – they just had to meet her where she already was.

items.desc: Computer simulations suggest comets carrying a key precursor to many of life's building blocks would have rarely—if ever—successfully reached Earth's surface. And even if they did, only specific landing conditions would have allowed the precursor molecule to drive biologically relevant reactions
items.text:
The question of how life started on Earth has proven to be almost as enigmatic as finding organisms on alien worlds. A longstanding theory posits that comets delivered the molecular ingredients that kickstarted life when they smacked into our planet during its youth. But new research suggests that this popular scenario is extremely unlikely.
In a study published October 28 in the journal Scientific Reports , researchers ran computer simulations of the celestial mail service and found that successful deliveries would have been rare, if not impossible. While the findings reorient discussions on the origin of life on Earth, they also posit a slightly more likely place where comets could’ve brought biologically useful organic molecules: our next-door neighbor, Mars.
The team investigated the potential delivery of hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule with hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen, that would’ve been made with leftovers from the solar system’s formation 4.6 billion years ago . It has been detected on many comets and can be a precursor for many of life’s essential building blocks, including lipids , sugars and nucleotides . That’s because the carbon-containing, or organic, molecule has an extremely strong chemical bond that can drive subsequent reactions. The bond also makes it very stable, and thus more likely than other organics to survive an impact.
“So, if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts,” lead author Richard Anslow , a planetary scientist who conducted the research at the University of Cambridge in England, tells Science News ’ Skyler Ware.
Comets , sometimes dubbed “dirty snowballs,” are masses of frozen gases, rock and dust located primarily in the outer solar system. When their orbit brings them closer to the sun, their materials get heated up and form a glowing head, as well as a tail that streaks across the sky.
And things did indeed look bad. Anslow and colleagues analyzed comet impact simulations, interactions between the atmosphere and comets, and models of the origin and evolution of comets. They found that comets likely wouldn’t have been able to supply enough HCN needed to seed life on Earth.

46 years ago today, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe arrived at Saturn and beamed back the first images ever taken of its rings. It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes.
But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.
“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement .
Roman campaigns into modern-day Scotland began in the 70s C.E., several decades after the conquest of Britain . Emperor Hadrian , who ruled from 117 C.E. to 138 C.E., consolidated the Romans’ northernmost limit in northern England, where Hadrian’s Wall still stands.
Hadrian’s successor, Antoninus Pius, pushed his armies north again, and in the early 140s C.E. fortified a position about 100 miles north of Hadrian’s Wall, known as the Antonine Wall . A few years after Antoninus Pius died in 161 C.E., the Roman armies retreated south, back to Hadrian’s Wall.
The timeline of the second century C.E. Roman invasion of southern Scotland—and eventual withdrawal—provides the context for the bronze limb.
Close inspection reveals that rather than bearing jagged axe or saw marks, the upper edge remains intact, just as Roman metalworkers originally cast it in the 140s C.E. An absence of gilding around the knee indicates that the leg was covered by a tunic or cloak, part of a larger statue, perhaps similar to the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome
“When you look, you see it hasn’t been hacked off, it’s a complete leg,” Hunter explains to the Telegraph ’s Ruby Cline. “So rather than loot, it looks as if the statue has been carefully decommissioned at the end of its life.”
When Roman forces abandoned southern Scotland, they routinely dismantled and buried prized monuments, including stone altars and inscriptions from the Antonine Wall, rather than leave them behind, per the statement.

A post shared by Region of Durham Paramedic Services (@durhamparamedic)
Being a paramedic takes a special kind of person. It calls for compassion, resilience, and the ability to stay calm when others are at their most vulnerable. Just one day on the job can take its toll, yet Durham, California-based paramedic Mike Nevill dedicated an incredible 59 years to the vital role. A recent viral video captures a heartwarming tribute made to Nevill as he sits in his ambulance for the last time before retiring.
As Nevill sits in the driver’s seat, he listens to a radio tribute from the dispatch team thanking him for his dedication and reflecting on his extraordinary career. Outside the ambulance, community members gather to show their support, while Nevill appears visibly emotional. The tribute also highlights how Nevill inspired his own daughter to follow in his footsteps and become a paramedic, “carrying forward the Nevill family tradition of caring for others.”
When sharing the video on Instagram , Durham Region Paramedic Services wrote in the caption, “Beginning his career in 1967, Mike dedicated a lifetime to caring for others, serving as a paramedic, supervisor, mentor and leader. His commitment extended beyond Durham, with decades of service in Kawartha Lakes and Northumberland County as well.” They added, “The number of lives Mike has touched throughout his record-breaking career is truly immeasurable. Thank you for your dedication, compassion and commitment to our profession and community.”
People online were quick to share their admiration for Nevill’s decades of service. One person wrote, “59 years of service ??? Paramedics have the hardest of all first responders, dude as a Firefighter my hat is off to you.” Another commented, “59 years as a paramedic! This man should never have to pay for a drink again.”
Let’s hope Nevill can now enjoy a well-deserved rest.

items.text:
In 1994, David vacationed on the Greek island of Kos with his family for a memorable week in which the English teen met a new pen pal.
There were 12 kids, all from different families, that became a friendly pack. One of them was Jodie, who was 15 at the time.
“You know how kids hang out on holiday, we were all just around the pool table and we decided to swap addresses and be pen pals.”
“Me and Jodie were the only ones that stayed in contact—and we carried on writing to each other for years. A letter every month or so, catching up.”
But after three years of communication, David moved, and the pair lost contact.
Little did they know that 29 years later they would get married.
David McArdle from Newcastle was two years older than Jodie, and they both went on their separate life paths.
It wasn’t until twenty years later that David saw a text message arrive on his mother’s phone from Jodie, saying ‘Happy birthday from me and the girls’.
“I couldn’t believe I found her again,” David told Talk to the Press. “I said to my mum, ‘I didn’t know you had Jodie’s number.’”
He replied to the text immediately (saying it was David) and, after a nail-biting 15-minute wait, Jodie, a teaching assistant, messaged back.
“She said she was so glad to hear from me.
“It turns out, that 15-minute wait for her reply was because she was sobbing her heart out looking at the text. She’d wanted to get in touch, but she thought I was in a relationship so she didn’t want to ruffle any feathers.”
From then on, the two never stop talking on the phone for two years, before eventually meeting in person, for the first time in 24 years, when David drove 300 miles to Cardiff to visit Jodie.
“We sat on the sofa and talked for 12 hours,” recalled David who visited her again two weeks later.
After three years of dating, David proposed at the top of the London Eye Ferris wheel and the pair were soon married.
Now the couple live together in Cardiff but visit Kos, the island they met on, every year in August, back to the apartments where they met and swapped addresses.
